tldr: We built an open-source framework using ROS 2 to integrate the compact, affordable 3-DOF Haply Inverse3 haptic device with the research-standard dVRK for haptic shared control. Through simulation and physical hardware experiments, we showed that simple linear guidance significantly reduces operational errors and task completion time.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the proposed haptic shared control system. The bridge node receives position and orientation inputs from the Haply Inverse3 via a ROS 2 driver, converts them into dVRK commands, and simultaneously feeds back guidance forces calculated from virtual environment interactions to the operator in real time.
overview:
Surgical robots like the da Vinci have revolutionized healthcare, but they carry a long-standing challenge: surgeons cannot directly feel tissue forces. While modern commercial platforms are beginning to restore force feedback, these systems remain completely closed. This prevents researchers from freely experimenting with custom collaborative control or haptic feedback algorithms.

Meanwhile, the dVRK (da Vinci Research Kit) is widely used in academia, but connected haptic master devices have been limited to a few extremely expensive high-end units. Open integration environments supporting modern ROS 2 have also been lacking. To address this, the research team focused on the Haply Inverse3, a compact, affordable 3-DOF haptic device gaining traction in education and research. By combining 3-DOF translational haptic feedback with an orientation-tracking stylus (VerseGrip), they developed a ROS 2-native control framework to intuitively operate the dVRK's 6-DOF Patient Side Manipulator (PSM).

Furthermore, as reference implementations for "shared control"—where the robot guides the operator along a desired trajectory—they integrated two guidance modes: simple linear stiffness guidance and two-stage progressive-stiffness guidance that pushes back harder toward the outer boundary. In an evaluation with 20 participants performing a simulated hot-wire benchmark task, simple linear guidance proved most effective. Compared to unassisted control, it significantly reduced wire contacts by about 34% and cut task completion time by about 22%. The team also validated the setup on physical dVRK hardware, dramatically lowering the barrier to entry for haptic assistance research.
contributions: Building an open-source, ROS 2-native communication and control architecture that integrates the compact Haply Inverse3 haptic device and VerseGrip with the dVRK
Proposing joint-space and Cartesian mapping strategies that combine 3-DOF force/position input with separate orientation tracking to smoothly drive the dVRK's 6-DOF arm
Implementing and comparing two virtual-fixture shared control algorithms (linear stiffness and two-stage progressive stiffness) matched in maximum displayable force
Validating the effectiveness of haptic guidance through a 20-participant user study and demonstrating real-time control on physical dVRK hardware

sections.heading: Why Connect an Affordable Haptic Device to a Surgical Robot Now?
sections.summary: The lack of force feedback in robot-assisted surgery introduces serious risks of excessive tissue damage. However, open platforms where researchers can freely test haptic shared control algorithms have remained limited.
sections.details:
One of the biggest shortcomings of robotic endoscopic surgery is that surgeons lose the tactile sensation of biological tissue. In clinical practice, surgeons infer forces from visual cues, such as tissue deformation, and prior experience. Yet this cannot fully eliminate the risk of injuring delicate tissue. While modern platforms like the da Vinci 5 are starting to feature force feedback, commercial systems remain black boxes. Researchers cannot use them to test custom collaborative control theories.

The dVRK has therefore been invaluable to the research community, but the master devices paired with it have mostly been extremely expensive systems, like Force Dimension's sigma.7. Integrating a more accessible and compact device like the Haply Inverse3 could broaden research participation significantly. However, because the Inverse3 is a 3-DOF translational haptic device, controlling a 6-DOF surgical instrument (position + orientation) and bridging it into a ROS 2 environment presented a major technical hurdle. This paper aims to deliver this system integration in an open-source format, providing an experimental platform for shared control.

sections.heading: From Force Display to Shared Control: Research Trends and Open Challenges
sections.summary: Research has shifted from simply reflecting environmental forces back to the user toward "shared control," which actively guides the operator along a correct path. However, skewed hardware accessibility and a lack of standard benchmarks have posed challenges.
sections.details:
### History of Haptics and Shared Control in Surgical Robotics
Past research focused primarily on achieving transparency through bilateral control, reflecting forces felt at the surgical site directly back to the surgeon. However, this approach has long struggled with miniaturization, sterilization constraints, and the trade-off between control stability and transparency. This led to the emergence of "haptic shared control." Rather than merely returning environmental reaction forces, the robot gently guides the operator's hand toward a predefined desired path. Using virtual fixtures (virtual walls or channels), this approach improves operational precision while letting the operator retain ultimate authority to override the system.

### Remaining Research Gaps
Despite these promising control theories, three major gaps remained in current research:
- First, most dVRK studies still rely on legacy middleware, with no prior work integrating a compact, affordable master device on top of modern ROS 2.
- Second, haptic research in surgical robotics has mostly focused on displaying environmental reaction forces, leaving collaborative guidance via shared control underexplored.
- Third, evaluation tasks vary widely across research labs, hindering objective comparison; standard benchmarks are needed to fairly evaluate path-following and collision-avoidance performance.

sections.heading: Steering a 6-DOF Arm with a 3-DOF Device: Inside the Integrated Architecture
sections.summary: The team developed a ROS 2 package that streams data from the Inverse3 and VerseGrip over WebSockets to drive the dVRK PSM. Joint-space mapping based on relative displacements avoids singularities while enabling intuitive control.
sections.details:
### ROS 2 Driver and Safety Design
Because the manufacturer does not provide an official ROS 2 driver, the authors developed a custom ROS 2 node wrapping the WebSocket-based API. It retrieves end-effector position and velocity from the Inverse3, along with quaternion orientations and button inputs from the VerseGrip stylus attachment in real time. The node supports both force-command and position-command (PID) control modes. For safety, it implements per-axis force saturation limits and a watchdog timer that instantly zeros the output if communication drops for 0.5 seconds.

### Coordinate Transforms and Mapping Strategies
The master side consists of 3-DOF translation from the Inverse3 and 3-DOF orientation from the VerseGrip. To convert this into 6-DOF commands for PSM1, the framework uses relative displacement mapping. It takes the state at the start of teleoperation as a baseline and scales displacements from that point before sending them to the robot.

Crucially, this work implements joint-space mapping alongside Cartesian mapping. The tool tip's lateral travel depends geometrically on the PSM insertion depth (joint 3, $q_3$). By setting a gain of $g = 10\,\mathrm{rad/m}$, the hand movement and tool movement intuitively match at an insertion depth of roughly 0.1 m. Sending these joint commands to the dVRK interpolated interface guarantees smooth motion.

### Clutching, Gripping, and Haptic Coordinate Transformation
Pressing button B on the VerseGrip resets only the translational reference position. This allows "clutching," letting the operator return the hand device to the center of its workspace without moving the physical arm. Button A toggles gripper opening and closing. Furthermore, guidance forces computed in virtual space are transformed into the Inverse3 coordinate frame via an orthogonal diagonal matrix ${\mathbf{S}}_z = \operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -1)$, rendering forces to the operator's hand in an energy-preserving manner.

captions.F1: Overall system architecture. The Haply driver captures the master state, and the bridge node applies joint-space mapping and shared-control logic to send commands to the dVRK (PSM1). The computed guidance forces are fed back to the operator's hand via the Inverse3.

sections.heading: Two Guidance Modes: Linear Stiffness vs. Two-Stage Progressive Stiffness
sections.summary: As reference shared-control implementations, the authors designed a linear mode (M1) returning forces proportional to deviation, and a progressive-stiffness mode (M2) that is soft near the center and stiffens sharply outward. Both modes were matched in maximum force for a fair comparison.
sections.details:
### Mode 1: Linear Stiffness Guidance (M1)
This is the most standard virtual fixture, returning a restoring force directly proportional to distance $d$ from the target trajectory (wire centerline). In addition to a spring constant of $k = 80\,\mathrm{N/m}$, a velocity damping coefficient of $b = 2\,\mathrm{N\cdot s/m}$ is introduced to prevent hand tremor and oscillation. The formulation is:
$$\mathbf{F} = k\,d\,\hat{\mathbf{n}} - b\,\mathbf{v}$$
where $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the unit normal vector pointing toward the nearest point on the target trajectory. At the outer active radius $d_o = 0.015\,\mathrm{m}$, the force reaches a maximum of roughly 1.2 N.

### Mode 2: Progressive-Stiffness Guidance (M2)
A single stiffness imposes a trade-off between delicate maneuverability near the center and reliable deviation prevention near the boundaries. In M2, the authors designed a piecewise-linear profile that switches stiffness at the midpoint radius $d_m = 0.0075\,\mathrm{m}$.
Near the center ($d \leq d_m$), stiffness is set lower at $k_1 = 40\,\mathrm{N/m}$ to allow free micro-manipulation. Closer to the boundary ($d > d_m$), stiffness jumps to $k_2 = 120\,\mathrm{N/m}$. Crucially, the parameters were analytically chosen so that the maximum force generated at the outermost boundary $d_o$ matches M1 exactly. This allows a rigorous comparison of how the shape of the haptic profile affects human operators, rather than just the strength of the force.

sections.heading: Taking on the Hot-Wire Task: A Rigorous Evaluation with 20 Participants
sections.summary: A user study was conducted with 20 participants across three conditions: unassisted (M0), linear (M1), and progressive stiffness (M2). Under a 2D monitor setup lacking depth cues, wire contacts, completion time, and subjective workload were evaluated.
sections.details:
### Experimental Design and Task Specifications
Twenty participants aged 25 to 65 (7 females, 13 males) took part, with teleoperation experience ranging from novices to advanced users. The task was a "hot-wire" benchmark, where participants guide a ring along a bent wire consisting of five straight segments with a total length of 0.21 m. The ring has an inner diameter of 0.02 m.

The study used a within-subjects design, where every participant completed all three modes: M0, M1, and M2. To balance order and learning effects, the presentation order was fully counterbalanced using a Latin square. Before testing each mode, participants had 5 minutes of practice (15 minutes total). Visual feedback was provided exclusively on a standard 2D monitor, testing how well haptic guidance can compensate when visual depth cues are lacking.

### Metrics and Hypotheses
Objective metrics included the number of wire contacts and task completion time. For subjective evaluation, participants completed a 7-point Likert questionnaire after the task assessing cognitive workload (Q1), sense of agency (Q2), and satisfaction (Q3). The authors hypothesized that haptic guidance (M1, M2) would significantly reduce contacts and completion times compared to M0, while significantly improving subjective experience.

sections.heading: Linear Guidance Dominates! Surprising Experimental Results and Statistical Significance
sections.summary: Linear mode (M1) significantly reduced contacts by about 34% and cut completion time by about 21 seconds compared to unassisted control (M0). Meanwhile, the more elaborate progressive mode (M2) showed improvement trends, but did not reach statistical significance.
sections.details:
### Objective Metrics: Contacts and Completion Time
The results were very clear. The mean number of contacts was 31.85 under unassisted M0, but dropped sharply to 20.90 under linear guidance M1. A paired t-test (with Bonferroni-corrected $\alpha = 0.025$) revealed a statistically significant difference with a medium-to-large effect size: $t(19) = 3.18, p = 0.005, d = 0.71$. Meanwhile, M2 showed a downward trend with an average of 24.35 contacts, but did not reach significance ($p = 0.130$).

Completion times showed a similar pattern. While M0 averaged 96.31 seconds, M1 achieved an average reduction of 21.3 seconds, finishing at 75.01 seconds ($t(19) = 3.45, p = 0.003, d = 0.77$, statistically significant). M2 remained intermediate at 84.25 seconds, showing no significant difference ($p = 0.098$).

### Subjective Metrics: Survey Trends
While Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for the subjective survey did not reveal statistically significant differences after correction for multiple comparisons, consistent positive trends emerged. Median cognitive workload (Q1) dropped from +2.0 in M0 to +1.0 in both M1 and M2. Sense of agency (Q2)—feeling in control of the motion—improved from -1.0 in M0 to +1.0 in M1 and +0.5 in M2. Satisfaction (Q3) also rose from -1.0 in M0 to 0.0 in both guidance modes.

sections.heading: Why Did Simple Linear Stiffness Outperform Complex Progressive Stiffness?
sections.summary: M2's softer center likely underperformed because sudden changes in stiffness imposed extra cognitive load on novices. A simple, predictable force field proved to be the most robust choice for assisting inexperienced teleoperators.
sections.details:
### Control Complexity and Cognitive Load
In theory, M2 sounds superior because it offers free movement near the center while firmly stopping deviations at the boundaries. In practice, however, simple M1 performed substantially better. The authors suggest that non-linear behavior with sudden force changes caused unexpected discomfort and cognitive load for inexperienced operators. For less experienced participants in particular, a linear spring (M1)—where restoring force increases at a constant rate with displacement—made forces intuitive to predict, allowing operators to comfortably rely on the assistance.

### Study Limitations
Several caveats apply when interpreting these results. First, the hot-wire task assesses basic teleoperation elements like path-following and collision avoidance; it does not directly evaluate clinical surgical skills such as suturing or dissection. Second, because a 2D monitor was used instead of a clinical 3D stereo endoscope, visual depth cues were absent. This may have exaggerated the benefits of haptic guidance compared to real clinical settings.

sections.heading: Demonstration on Physical dVRK Hardware: From Simulation to Real Surgical Robot
sections.summary: Connecting the developed framework to physical dVRK hardware confirmed stable real-time haptic shared control. Achieving a 1 kHz control rate, the system demonstrated smooth operation without oscillations or latency issues.
sections.details:
### Hardware Setup and Real-Time Performance
The research team deployed the exact same software stack validated in simulation directly onto physical dVRK hardware (PSM1). While the Inverse3 supports haptic update rates up to 4 kHz, the system was fully synchronized at 1 kHz to match the dVRK control loop.

Key findings from the physical experiments include:
- **Tracking Accuracy**: Because the Inverse3 has an extremely fine position resolution of 0.01 mm, overall system tracking error was dominated by the dVRK's inherent accuracy (about 1 to 2 mm), meaning the master device caused no bottleneck.
- **Latency and Stability**: The setup maintained smooth communication without worsening teleoperation latency past the accepted upper threshold of roughly 200 ms. Moreover, the viscous damping term ($b = 2\,\mathrm{N\cdot s/m}$) functioned effectively, preventing hand oscillations and triggering no watchdog force shutoffs.

When operators held the Inverse3 to guide the ring along a physical wire, video demonstrations confirmed they could smoothly follow the path while clearly perceiving restoring forces from the virtual walls.

captions.F5: Experimental setup on physical hardware. On the left is the Haply Inverse3 haptic device held by the operator; on the right is the physical dVRK manipulator tip executing the hot-wire task.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Outlook: Toward an Accessible Surgical Haptics Research Ecosystem
sections.summary: The open-source ROS 2 framework integrating the Haply Inverse3 with the dVRK proved its utility. Future directions include integrating VR stereo displays and extending to adaptive shared control based on game theory.
sections.details:
This paper presented an open-source ROS 2 framework that integrates the affordable, compact 3-DOF Haply Inverse3 haptic device with the dVRK, validating its effectiveness through both simulation and physical hardware experiments. In particular, the finding that simple linear haptic guidance outperforms elaborate non-linear control in reducing errors and saving time for novice operators offers practical guidance for future shared-control design.

Future work points to integrating immersive stereo VR displays closer to clinical setups, developing adaptive shared control that tunes intervention levels based on real-time estimates of operator expertise or cognitive workload (such as via potential differential game theory), and evaluating more realistic surgical tasks with tissue phantoms. Releasing the entire software stack as open source (under the MIT license) is expected to significantly lower the barrier for researchers worldwide to enter advanced haptic shared control research.

takeaways: Even an affordable, compact 3-DOF device can serve effectively as a master controller for 6-DOF surgical robot shared control when paired with an appropriate mapping design.
In shared control stiffness design, a simple linear spring profile improves operator predictability and significantly reduces errors and time compared to elaborate multi-stage profiles.
Releasing a ROS 2-native, open-source stack that interfaces with the dVRK dramatically lowers research and development costs for haptic feedback and shared control.
limitations: Visual feedback in the experiments was limited to a 2D monitor, which may have led participants to rely more heavily on haptic guidance than they would under true 3D stereoscopic vision.
The evaluation was restricted to a hot-wire task (geometric trajectory following) and did not assess specific surgical skills such as tissue interaction, cutting, or dissection.
Participants had varied backgrounds in teleoperation experience, and subjective ratings did not reach statistical significance after Bonferroni correction.
